Bank of England holds interest rates at 4% as inflation stays sticky

Published 2026-10-07 11:00 UTC

The Bank of England has left interest rates unchanged at 4%, saying UK inflation is falling more slowly than hoped. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 6-3 to hold, with three members backing a cut to 3.75%.

Inflation in the UK was 3.8% in August, almost double the Bank's 2% target, driven by food prices and household energy bills. The governor, Andrew Bailey, said rates were likely to continue on a gradual downward path but that the Bank needed to be sure inflation would return to target.

Mortgage lenders had already priced in a hold. Economists expect the next cut in February. The pound edged higher against the dollar after the announcement, and the FTSE 100 was little changed.

The Bank's monetary policy committee voted 6-3 to keep the base rate unchanged, with three members preferring a cut to 3.75%. Policymakers said inflation, at 3.6%, remains well above the 2% target, driven by food prices and services costs, and that they need more evidence it is falling before lowering borrowing costs again.

Governor said the committee expects inflation to fall back towards the target next year as energy price rises drop out of the annual comparison, but that wage growth remains strong enough to keep services inflation sticky. The Bank's forecasts suggest the economy will grow by about 1% this year.

Homeowners on tracker mortgages will see no change to their payments, and fixed-rate deals are expected to stay roughly where they are. Savers will continue to benefit from relatively high interest rates on deposit accounts, although many easy-access accounts pay less than inflation.

Business groups urged the Bank to cut rates soon, arguing that high borrowing costs are holding back investment and that firms face rising costs from higher employer national insurance contributions. Unions said households are still struggling with high prices and that lower rates would ease pressure on mortgage holders.

Markets expect the Bank to cut rates at its next meeting in November, especially if inflation figures due later this month show further easing.
